comments.comment: 3:26 Something you appear to have missed. Cooper must have had intricate knowledge of the aircraft, as he specifically instructed the pilot to fly with the landing gear down, the flaps at 15 degrees, and below 10,000ft. This was done to slow the cruising speed of the aircraft and make the jump possible. Importantly ( and what you've seemingly overlooked) the Boeing 727 was the only commercial aircraft capable of doing this, and Northwest Orient Airlines the only airline operating that plane at that time in that region.   The plane and airline were purposely chosen for that. Not solely for the aft stairway.   Given this knowledge, Cooper must have known the flight would need to refuel en route to Mexico. I don't believe that was an oversight at all. I think it was inconsequential to him where they refueled as he knew exactly when he would make his jump.   Supposition: Depending on when he deployed the canopy, from 10,000ft his jump would have been somewhere between 35 and 55 seconds free fall, before deployment, and about 4 to 5 mins canopy drop time. Estimate 6 minutes total. He could easily have survived that without a jump suit. It's also possible he'd carried some sort of overall either to jump in, or to (dry) change into on landing. Additionally, someone so well informed  would have prepared for landing and may possibly had ground support which he contacted by a hand held radio.   Had a radio been stowed in the bomb case, i seriously doubt the cabin crew would have even noticed. Perceptual narrowing would have meant they focused solely on the dynamite.
